titre: New Zealand (1893): “First Country” to Vote, Provided You Read “Country”
accroche: New Zealand is said to be the “first country” to give women the vote in 1893: Wyoming, then a territory, had done so twenty-four years earlier.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 28, 1893, New Zealand women voted for the first time in a general election; the women voters of the separate Maori districts voted in turn on the following December 20. New Zealand enters the textbooks as “the first country in the world” to have granted women the right to vote: a formula that is true, but that rests on one word that is rarely set aside: *country*.

## A 270-Meter Petition

The outcome was the fruit of a campaign of several years, led by the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which Kate Sheppard had headed since 1887. On July 28, 1893, the member of Parliament Sir John Hall presented to Parliament a petition gathering nearly 32,000 signatures: the largest ever presented up to then, made up of more than 500 sheets pasted into a roll more than 270 meters long. The resulting text, the *Electoral Act 1893*, cleared the upper house on September 8, then received royal assent from Governor Lord Glasgow on September 19, 1893.

## First Country, Not First Jurisdiction

Before 1893, however, other jurisdictions had already let women vote. The American territory of Wyoming granted women's suffrage as early as December 10, 1869, twenty-four years earlier (the first women voters there voted in 1870), but it was then only a territory, which would not become a state until 1890. The Isle of Man, which has its own parliament, opened the vote to certain women in 1881, according to a property or residence criterion that sources describe differently. New Zealand therefore remains, more precisely, the first **self-governing country** where all women aged 21 and over could vote in parliamentary elections: already a considerable distinction, but narrower than the shortened formula that keeps being repeated.

It has its own limits: the law applies to British subjects, which includes Maori women, but excludes “aliens,” among them Chinese migrant women who had not applied for naturalization.

The reform itself also has a silent limit: voting is not standing for office. New Zealand women would not be able to run for Parliament themselves until 1919, twenty-six years later. South Australia, in 1895, by contrast opened both rights at the same time: proof that the order in which a society grants the right to vote and the right to be elected is in no way automatic, and that the victory made possible by Kate Sheppard and tens of thousands of signers did not, by itself, settle the whole question of representation.

repere.texte: The petition presented to the New Zealand Parliament on July 28, 1893 gathered nearly 32,000 signatures on more than 500 sheets pasted into a roll more than 270 meters long.

carte.punch: New Zealand (1893), the “first country” to vote, but Wyoming had done so 24 years earlier.
carte.idee: In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country where all women aged 21 and over could vote in parliamentary elections. The territory of Wyoming (1869) and the Isle of Man (1881) had preceded it, for some women, without the right to be elected.

quiz.question: Why does the formula “New Zealand, the first country to give women the vote” call for a clarification?
choix: Because New Zealand women actually voted only from 1919
Because Wyoming and the Isle of Man had already opened the vote to women
Because it was actually South Australia that passed the law first
Because the 1893 petition was never examined by the New Zealand Parliament
quiz.explication: Wyoming (1869, a mere territory) and the Isle of Man (1881, for some women) had already opened the vote to women; New Zealand is the first self-governing country where all women aged 21 and over could vote in parliamentary elections. They voted from 1893, not 1919 (the date they became eligible to stand), and the petition was indeed presented to Parliament.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who heads the Women's Christian Temperance Union from 1887, leading the campaign that results in the 1893 law?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that Kate Sheppard has headed the Women's Christian Temperance Union since 1887; Sir John Hall presents the petition and Lord Glasgow gives royal assent, but they do not lead the campaign.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What limit affects the 1893 New Zealand electoral law itself, according to the entry?
choix: It excludes Maori women from the ballot
It reserves the vote for property owners
It forbids married women to vote
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The law applies to British subjects, which includes Maori women, but excludes non-naturalized aliens, among them Chinese migrant women, the entry specifies.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What distinguishes South Australia (1895) from New Zealand (1893), according to the entry?
choix: It granted women the vote twenty years earlier
It never allowed women to vote
It opened the vote and eligibility at the same time
It reserved the vote for single women
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry notes that South Australia opens both rights at once in 1895, whereas in New Zealand women would not be able to run for office themselves until 1919.
